chapters.title: Chapter 1: What History Means by a Cycle

lessons.title: Credit and Interest Rates: The Engine Behind Every Cycle

body.text: Emotion decides which way a market wants to move. Credit decides how far it can go. Cheap, easy borrowing stretches booms far beyond what earnings justify, and when the borrowing has to be repaid, it turns an ordinary fall into a forced sale.

children.text: Lesson 1.2 ended with an observation: the inventory, investment and real estate cycles all run on borrowed money. This lesson looks at that engine directly. It covers how leverage magnifies both gains and losses, how a whole economy moves through a credit cycle, the economist who explained why long periods of stability breed instability, and the simple link between interest rates and what investors will pay for a share. Chapter 4 goes deeper into RBI interest rate cycles. Here the goal is to understand the mechanism.

Start with one investor. Priya has ₹1,00,000 to invest in a stock. She can use only her own money, or she can borrow another ₹1,00,000 at 10% interest for a year and invest ₹2,00,000. Here is what happens if the stock rises or falls 20% over that year.

body.caption: Same stock, same 20% move, different outcome with borrowed money (interest of ₹10,000 on the loan for one year)

children.text: Borrowing turned a 20% gain into 30%, and a 20% loss into 50%. The interest is owed either way, which is why the downside grows faster than the upside. Now multiply Priya by millions of investors, companies, developers and lenders. When borrowing is cheap and prices are rising, leverage makes everyone look brilliant and encourages more of it. When prices fall, the same leverage wipes out equity quickly and forces people to sell, which pushes prices down further.

body.title: Show me the math: when does the margin call arrive?

children.text: Suppose Priya's ₹2,00,000 position is funded with ₹1,00,000 borrowed from her broker, and the broker requires her own equity to stay at 40% or more of the position's value. Her equity is the position value minus the loan. Ignoring interest for simplicity, the margin call comes when:

content.caption: x is the percentage fall in the stock, written as a decimal

children.text: Solving gives a position value of about ₹1,66,667, which is a fall of about 16.7%. Priya's equity at that point is about ₹66,667, exactly 40% of the position. A fall of only one sixth triggers a demand for more cash or a forced sale. In a market-wide decline, thousands of these forced sales hit the market together.

body.title: Calculate the Damage
body.prompt: Arjun has ₹50,000 of his own money and borrows ₹1,00,000 to buy ₹1,50,000 of shares. The shares fall 25%. Ignoring interest, what percentage of Arjun's own money has he lost?
body.explanation: The position falls to ₹1,50,000 × 0.75 = ₹1,12,500. After repaying the ₹1,00,000 loan, Arjun is left with ₹12,500. He started with ₹50,000, so he has lost ₹37,500, which is 75%. A 25% fall in the stock became a 75% loss for him, because he was leveraged three times. Add interest and it is worse.

children.text: The Credit Cycle in Four Stages

markDefs.definition: The interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends short-term money to banks. It is the RBI's main policy rate, and changes in it flow through to loan and deposit rates across the economy.

children.text: At the level of the whole economy, credit moves in a loop. The central bank sets the price of money through its

, but lenders' willingness to lend and borrowers' appetite to borrow matter just as much. Rising asset prices make collateral look more valuable, which justifies more lending, which pushes asset prices higher still. The loop runs in reverse on the way down.

body.caption: The four stages of a credit cycle

cells: Rates are cut, banks are cautious after past losses, borrowers are nervous
Rates stay low, lending picks up, defaults are rare
Lending standards slip, riskier borrowers get loans easily, central bank starts raising rates
Euphoria. "Debt is cheap, why not borrow more?"
Defaults rise, banks pull back, borrowers are forced to sell
Fear. "Get me out at any price."

body.title: RBI repo rate at major turning points, 2008 to 2025

children.text: The chart shows only the peaks and troughs of each rate cycle, so the points are not evenly spaced in time. Notice the rhythm: sharp cuts in crises (2008 to 2009, 2020), followed by hikes once inflation returns (2010 to 2011, 2022 to 2023). Each of those turns changed what borrowers paid on home loans, business loans and margin funding, and markets reacted to them. Check the RBI website for the current repo rate, since it may have moved since this lesson was written.

The American economist Hyman Minsky, who died in 1996, spent his career arguing something unpopular: financial crises are not caused by outside shocks alone, they build up inside the system during the good years. Long periods of calm persuade borrowers and lenders that risk has fallen, so they take on more debt with thinner safety margins. His financial instability hypothesis sorts borrowers into three types, and the mix shifts as a boom matures.

cells: A salaried buyer in Bengaluru whose home loan EMI is a comfortable share of take-home pay
Interest only. Principal must be refinanced when due
Lenders continuing to roll over the debt
A lender funding long-term loans with short-term commercial paper that must be renewed every few months
Asset prices continuing to rise so the asset can be sold at a profit
An investor paying margin interest on a loss-making small-cap, relying purely on the price going up

children.text: As a boom runs on, more borrowers drift from hedge to speculative to Ponzi finance. Eventually something small, a rate hike or one large default, makes lenders refuse to roll over debt. Speculative and Ponzi borrowers are forced to sell assets, prices fall, and even hedge borrowers get hurt. The sudden turn is now widely called a Minsky moment, a term coined by fund manager Paul McCulley in 1998.

body.title: An Indian Minsky moment: the NBFC crisis of 2018 to 2019

events.title: Easy funding
events.description: Non-banking finance companies grow loan books rapidly, especially to real estate developers. Many fund long-term loans with cheap short-term borrowing from mutual funds and banks. NBFC stocks become market favourites.

events.title: IL&FS defaults
events.description: Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services, a group with debt of over ₹90,000 crore and a high credit rating until shortly before, defaults on its obligations. The government takes control of its board soon after.

events.title: Lenders refuse to roll over
events.description: Mutual funds and banks cut exposure to NBFCs almost overnight. Companies that depended on renewing short-term debt, speculative borrowers in Minsky's terms, suddenly cannot. Shares of DHFL and other housing finance companies collapse.

events.title: Fallout
events.description: Real estate developers lose a key source of funding and project delays spread. DHFL becomes the first financial services company referred to insolvency proceedings under the IBC, and is later acquired by Piramal.

body.title: Classify the Borrower
body.question: A real estate developer's rental and sales income covers the interest on its loans, but not the principal. It plans to repay the principal by taking a fresh loan when the current one matures in two years. In Minsky's framework, which type of borrower is this?
options: Hedge, because income covers the interest
Speculative, because it depends on lenders refinancing the principal
Ponzi, because it cannot repay anything
None, because Minsky's framework only applies to banks
body.explanation: Covering interest but relying on refinancing to repay principal is speculative finance. It works as long as lenders are willing, and fails badly when credit tightens at the wrong moment, as many NBFC borrowers found in 2018.

body.label: Regulators watch the credit cycle too
body.value: RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer loans in November 2023
body.context: After rapid growth in personal loans and credit card debt, the RBI made banks and NBFCs hold more capital against unsecured consumer lending, and against bank loans to NBFCs. It was a deliberate move to cool one part of the credit cycle before it reached the excess stage.

children.text: Interest Rates and What You Pay for a Share

Lesson 1.1 showed that the P/E multiple drives most of a market cycle. Interest rates are one of the biggest reasons that multiple moves. Flip the P/E ratio upside down and you get the earnings yield: the profit you are buying for every ₹100 you invest. That number competes directly with what a bank fixed deposit or a government bond pays.

body.caption: A P/E of 20 means an earnings yield of 5%

children.text: When a safe fixed deposit pays 5%, a stock market on a P/E of 25, an earnings yield of 4%, is easy to justify, because earnings are expected to grow. When fixed deposits pay 9%, the same 4% earnings yield looks much less attractive, and investors demand a lower P/E before they buy. Rising rates pull multiples down. Falling rates push them up. The relationship is loose and far from mechanical, and Chapter 4 looks at how it has actually played out in India, but the direction is consistent enough to matter.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: If the Nifty 50 trades at a P/E of 25, its earnings yield is ___%.
body.explanation: Earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E = 1 ÷ 25 = 0.04, or 4%. Compare that with what a 10-year government bond or a bank fixed deposit is paying at the time to judge how richly the market is priced.

columns.label: Easy credit phase
points: Banks and NBFCs growing loans quickly
Leveraged businesses and borrowers look like winners

columns.label: Tight credit phase
points: Lenders cutting back and tightening standards
Leveraged businesses and borrowers are hit first and hardest

body.title: Signs the Credit Cycle Is Getting Stretched
steps: Loan growth, especially unsecured personal loans and credit cards, running far faster than income growth in the economy
Lenders advertising instant, paperless loans to borrowers with thin credit histories
Brokers heavily promoting margin trading and leveraged products, and rising margin funding balances
Companies funding long-term assets with short-term borrowing
Regulators such as the RBI or SEBI stepping in to tighten rules on specific kinds of lending or leverage
People around you borrowing to invest because "the returns are higher than the interest"

body.title: The Margin Trading Temptation
body.scenario: Your cousin, 26 and working in Hyderabad, has ₹2 lakh in shares on Zerodha. The market has been rising steadily for two years and the repo rate has just been cut. He notices his broker offers a margin trading facility that would let him buy roughly twice as much stock, paying interest on the borrowed portion. He says: "Rates are falling, the market is strong, and the interest is small compared with what I'm making."
body.prompt: Using the ideas in this lesson, explain what could go wrong and where he sits in Minsky's framework.
body.modelAnswer: He is describing the excess stage of a credit cycle from the inside: rising prices, cheaper money and a belief that the return will comfortably beat the interest. At twice leverage, a 20% fall would cost him roughly 40% of his own money before interest, and a fall of well under 20% could trigger a margin call, forcing him to add cash or sell at a low price. His plan to cover the interest depends on the shares continuing to rise, since his salary is not what he is counting on to repay the loan, which puts this position close to Minsky's Ponzi category. Falling rates also do not guarantee rising prices: rate cuts often come because growth is weakening. Two years of gains say little about the next year. If he wants more equity exposure, the cycle-aware way is to add his own savings gradually, not to borrow against a portfolio at a point when easy credit is making everyone feel safe.

cards.definition: Using borrowed money to increase the size of an investment. It magnifies both gains and losses on your own capital.
A demand from a lender or broker to add cash or securities when your own equity in a leveraged position falls below the required level. If you cannot, the position is sold.
The RBI's main policy rate, at which it lends short-term money to banks.
Hyman Minsky's idea that long periods of stability encourage more and riskier borrowing, which makes the financial system more fragile.
The point at which lenders stop rolling over debt and over-borrowed investors are forced to sell, starting a sharp fall in asset prices.
EPS divided by price, or 1 ÷ P/E. It lets you compare what equities earn with what bonds and fixed deposits pay.

body.label: RBI: Current Policy Rates
body.description: The RBI homepage shows the current repo rate and other policy rates. Its monetary policy statements explain why rates were changed, which is the best first-hand record of where India is in the rate cycle.

children.text: That completes the toolkit for this course: cycles exist, several of them overlap, and credit is the fuel that stretches them. Chapter 2 puts the toolkit to work on history, starting with the first recorded speculative manias in Holland, Britain and the railway age.

body.text: Examples in this lesson, including the margin trading scenario, are for education only and are not recommendations to borrow, trade or invest. Leveraged products can cause losses larger than your original investment. Policy rates and regulatory rules change over time, so check current figures with the RBI and SEBI, and consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for advice on your own situation.

points: Leverage magnifies both directions: with ₹1 lakh of your own money and ₹1 lakh borrowed at 10%, a 20% rise becomes +30% and a 20% fall becomes −50%
A position funded half by a broker, with a 40% equity requirement, triggers a margin call after a fall of only about 16.7%
The credit cycle moves through repair, expansion, excess and contraction, and rising asset prices feed more lending until the loop reverses
Minsky showed that stability breeds instability, as borrowers drift from hedge to speculative to Ponzi finance during a long boom
India's 2018 NBFC crisis, triggered by the IL&FS default, is a textbook Minsky moment: lenders refused to roll over short-term debt
Earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E. Higher interest rates make a given earnings yield less attractive, which tends to pull market multiples down
